421.title: Alone, not lonely
421.hook: being alone isn't loneliness; learn to be at ease by yourself (Discourses 3.13)
421.carry: someone you can live with is there
421.howItsDone: Some people drawn to Stoicism set aside a short time each day to be alone without distractions, treating it as practice in being at ease with themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday: askēsis, and your line, privately. Did you keep one piece of training entirely to yourself? Day four hundred twenty-one.

A party of two hundred people can be lonelier than a quiet walk by yourself. Some people who live alone are deeply at ease, while some who are never alone feel stranded. A full calendar doesn't promise company, and an empty room doesn't promise loneliness. Being by yourself and feeling forlorn turn out to be two different things. Epictetus heard people in crowded Rome say they'd been left all alone. Today: alone, not lonely.
screen: `LONELY AT A PARTY OF TWO HUNDRED.` → `AT EASE ON A QUIET WALK.` → `FORLORN IN A GREAT CITY.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book three, chapter thirteen: what solitude is. Epictetus starts by separating two things we usually blur together. Being alone, he says, doesn't make someone forlorn, any more than being in a crowd makes them not forlorn. When we lose a brother, a child or a friend, we say we've been left all alone, even while we're living in Rome, with crowds in the street and neighbors on every side. So what is the forlorn feeling, really? Epictetus says it's being without help, exposed, at the mercy of whatever comes. Then he reaches for an image from Stoic belief about the cosmos. In the Stoic picture he's drawing on, the world goes through cycles, and at the end of each it's drawn back into fire. In that moment, Zeus is alone. Yet he isn't forlorn. He's at rest with himself, thinking about how things are ordered. We should be able to do something like that, Epictetus says: to talk with ourselves, to not need others in order to be at peace, to not be lost when there's no one to fill the hours. He adds a contrast. The emperor, he says, gives the world a great peace: no wars, no pirates, safe roads. But the emperor can't give peace from fever, shipwreck, grief or envy. That inner peace, Epictetus says, has to be learned. And one of its first lessons is learning to sit in an empty room and find that someone you can live with is there.

segments.voice: Sit somewhere you can be by yourself, even if it's just a corner. Breathe. Notice whether being alone feels restful, or a little uneasy, or both. Don't reach for your phone. Just keep yourself company. Ask, gently, as if talking to a friend: how are you, really? Listen for the answer. Then let the quiet be enough for a while. If you can, give yourself ten minutes like this later today. The bell holds the time.
Alone. Epictetus on solitude: being by yourself isn't the same as being forlorn, and we can learn to be at ease in our own company.
Your line: someone you can live with is there. Take ten minutes alone today, no screen, no task, and practice being at ease with yourself. Day four hundred twenty-one.

422.title: The scout
422.hook: a long portrait of the Cynic as scout and witness, sent to report what's really good
422.howItsDone: People who practice Stoicism often try to separate what happened from what they added to it, and to describe events to others plainly, the way Epictetus' scout reports the ground.

segments.voice: Yesterday: alone, not lonely, and your line, someone you can live with is there. Did you find your ten minutes by yourself, and were they easy or itchy? Day four hundred twenty-two.
screen: `SOMEONE YOU CAN LIVE WITH IS THERE.`

segments.voice: Before an ancient army moved, it sent a few people ahead. They went quietly into the hills, looked at the ground, counted the campfires on the far side of the valley, and came back to say what was really there. Everything hung on that report. A scout who panicked and said a thousand enemies when there were ten could send a whole army running from nothing. Epictetus loved this picture. In one of the longest talks in the Discourses, book three, chapter twenty-two, he uses it to describe a certain kind of philosopher. Today: the scout.
screen: `SENT AHEAD INTO THE HILLS.` → `COUNT THE FIRES. COME BACK.` → `THE SCOUT.`

segments.voice: First, the Cynics. They were a Greek movement usually traced back more than four centuries before Epictetus, to Diogenes of Sinope, who lived on almost nothing: a rough cloak, a bag, a staff, and a large storage jar to sleep in. Their name most likely comes from kyon, the Greek word for dog. It seems to have started as an insult, and they wore it on purpose. Second, the scout. Epictetus says the true Cynic is sent ahead, like a scout, to find out what is friendly to human beings and what is hostile, and then to come back and report it truthfully. Not frightened into a false report. Not dazzled into one either. And the report is this: people are hunting for happiness where it isn't, in money, office and the good opinion of others, and it lives in their own choices. Third, the warning. Most of that long chapter is a warning. A young man asks about taking up the Cynic life, and Epictetus tells him, in effect, don't you dare do it lightly. The cloak and the staff are the easy part. The real Cynic has nothing to hide, keeps his mind clean, takes a beating without hating the one who gives it, and cares for everyone the way a father or a brother would. Fourth, the witness. In book one, Epictetus says Diogenes was sent out as a scout and came back with a calm report: death is no evil, because it isn't shameful. Elsewhere he calls the philosopher a witness, someone whose own life shows that you can lose what the world prizes and still be well. You don't need a cloak for the small version. A scout simply looks at what's there and says so.

segments.voice: Think of one thing you'll report on today: how a meeting went, how your kid's day was, how a parent seemed on the phone. Bring it to mind. Notice the report you'd usually give, the one shaped by worry, or by wanting to look good. Then ask, slowly: what did I actually see, and what did I add? Let the two come apart, the way oil and water settle in a glass. Breathe, and hold only the plain report, the ten fires, no more and no less. The bell holds the time.
The scout. Epictetus' picture of the philosopher sent ahead to see what is truly good and bad, and to come back and report it honestly, without fear. Today's word.
Your line: a scout. Once today, when someone asks how something went, give the plain report: what you saw, nothing added, nothing hidden. Be a good witness once. Day four hundred twenty-two.

423.title: In its season
423.hook: figs come in season and go, and so do the people we love
423.carry: receive the season while it lasts
423.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism remind themselves, gently, that the people they love are with them for a time, and use that reminder to be more present and more grateful rather than more anxious.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the scout, sent ahead to count the fires and report plainly. Did you give one plain report, nothing added? Day four hundred twenty-three.

A fig tree, a peach tree, a strawberry patch at a farm stand: for a few weeks each summer the fruit is perfect, and then it's gone. Nobody stands under a bare fig tree in January shouting at it. We know how fruit works. Epictetus thought we forget that knowledge the moment it's a person. In a long talk where he tells us not to be moved by what isn't ours, book three, chapter twenty-four, he reaches for the fig. Today: fig.
screen: `A FEW PERFECT WEEKS.` → `NOBODY YELLS AT A BARE TREE.` → `IN ITS SEASON.`

segments.voice: First, the fig in winter. Epictetus says that to long for a friend or a child when they're no longer given to you is like longing for a fig in winter. Not wicked. Just out of season. The tree was never going to give fruit in the snow, and wanting it doesn't change the tree. Second, the kiss. Then he says something that makes people wince. When you kiss your child, he says, you might quietly tell yourself: tomorrow you may die. Someone objects at once: that's an ill-omened thing to say. Third, his answer. Is it ill-omened, he asks, to say that the grain will be harvested? That leaves fall? That a fresh fig becomes a dried one, and a grape a raisin? These are only changes, things moving from one state to the next. Nothing in nature is cursed by being named. The point of the whisper isn't to spoil the kiss. It's to make it real, to kiss a living person who is here now, rather than a permanent possession you assume you'll always have. Fourth, the gift. What we love, Epictetus says, has been given to us for the present, not forever, like a fig or a bunch of grapes in its season. So the right response isn't to clutch, and it isn't to stop loving. It's to receive the season while it lasts, and when it ends, one fitting answer is thanks. Ecclesiastes says it too, in its own way: there is a season for everything. Epictetus says it with a fig.
screen: `A FIG IN WINTER.` · `THE WHISPER DURING THE KISS.` · `NAMING CHANGE IS NOT A CURSE.` · `RECEIVE IT, THEN SAY THANK YOU.` · then, large: `IN ITS SEASON.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone whose season with you has changed. A grandparent. A friend from an old job. A teacher. Someone who moved away, or grew up, or died. Picture one ordinary moment with them, the kitchen, the car, the bench. Let that season be there for a moment. Now, silently or under your breath, simply say: thank you for that season. If they're still reachable, you might decide now to tell them later today. If not, let the thanks rest where it is. The bell holds the time.
Fig. Epictetus' image for what we love: given for a time, like a fig in its season, so we receive it while it's here and give thanks when it passes.
Your line: receive the season while it lasts. Today, thank one person, out loud or in a message, for the season they've been in your life. Say what it was. Day four hundred twenty-three.

424.title: At home here
424.hook: Odysseus wept for home on Calypso's island; Heracles was at home anywhere
424.howItsDone: Stoic writers, Epictetus among them, speak of being citizens of the world, and some practitioners make a habit of settling into wherever they are, treating any place as a place where they can act well.

segments.voice: Yesterday: fig, the fig that comes and goes, and your line, receive the season while it lasts. Did you thank someone for the season they were in your life? Day four hundred twenty-four.

A man sits on a rock at the edge of the sea, staring at the horizon, crying. He's on a beautiful island. A goddess loves him and has offered him a life without death. He doesn't care. Day after day he goes down to the shore and weeps for a rocky little kingdom he hasn't seen in years. That's Odysseus, in book five of Homer's Odyssey, on Calypso's island. Epictetus picked it up and asked an awkward question about it. Today: at home here.
screen: `A MAN ON A ROCK, CRYING.` → `CALYPSO'S ISLAND.` → `AT HOME HERE.`

segments.voice: First, the weeping. Epictetus, in that same long chapter of book three, asks whether we should take Homer at his word in everything. If Odysseus really sat and wept like that, he says, then he was unhappy, not living well. Homer may have told it that way, but a person who can only be happy in one spot on the map has handed their happiness to geography. Epictetus isn't mocking homesickness. He's asking where we've put our peace. Second, the other hero. Then he turns to Heracles. In the old stories Heracles traveled the whole known world on his labors, clearing out cruelty and lawlessness wherever he went. Epictetus says he made friends in every place, had children in more than one land, and left them without groaning, not because he didn't love them, but because he believed every human being was his kin, and Zeus the father of all. Third, the old phrase. It's the citizen of the world we met on the day of names, onoma. Diogenes the Cynic, asked where he was from, is said to have answered: I'm a citizen of the world, a kosmopolitēs. Fourth, what it isn't. It isn't a rule against missing home. Epictetus doesn't say don't love your city, your street, your mother's kitchen. He says don't make them the only place you can stand up straight. Wherever there are people, sky and a chance to act well, there is work for you to do. A hospital waiting room, a new apartment, a strange city at night. You can be at home there too.
screen: `ODYSSEUS WEEPS ON THE ROCK.` · `HERACLES IS AT HOME ANYWHERE.` · `A CITIZEN OF THE WORLD.` · `LOVE HOME; DON'T NEED ONLY IT.` · then, large: `AT HOME HERE.`

segments.voice: Wherever you are right now, a bedroom, a bus, a break room, let your eyes move slowly around it. Notice the light. Notice one thing someone made with their hands: a chair, a window, a cup. Feel what's holding you up, the seat or the floor. Breathe in this air, the air of exactly here. And quietly tell yourself: this, too, is a place where a person can live well. You don't have to love it. Just let yourself stand in it, at home for these two minutes. The bell holds the time.
At home here. The Stoic picture of Heracles, kin to every person in every land, set against Odysseus weeping on his rock: peace that doesn't depend on one spot on the map. Today's word.

Your line: at home here. The next time you're somewhere you'd rather not be, a line, an office, a waiting room, say it once under your breath and look for one good thing to do there. Day four hundred twenty-four.

425.title: Free is wanting rightly
425.hook: the free person lives as they wish, which means wishing rightly
425.carry: same person, same day, different leash
425.howItsDone: Stoic practice often means sorting a desire into the part that depends on oneself and the part that doesn't, and putting one's effort and hope on the first part.

segments.voice: Yesterday: at home here, Heracles at ease in every land. Did you say it once somewhere you'd rather not be? Day four hundred twenty-five.

Ask what freedom means, and a common answer is: doing what I want. No boss. No curfew. Nobody telling me what to do. It's a fine answer. Epictetus starts a long talk with almost the same definition, and then pulls a thread until the whole sweater comes apart. Book four, chapter one, is called On Freedom. He had a stake in the question: elsewhere in the Discourses he mentions the master he once had. Today: eleutheria.
screen: `FREEDOM: DOING WHAT I WANT?` → `ON FREEDOM, BOOK FOUR.` → `FREE IS WANTING RIGHTLY.`

segments.voice: First, the definition. Epictetus opens: the free person is the one who lives as they wish, who can't be forced, or blocked, or compelled. Second, the thread. Then he asks: does anyone wish to live in error? To be deceived, unjust, frightened, out of control? No one does. So anyone who lives that way is not living as they wish. And if they aren't living as they wish, by the first definition, they aren't free. Freedom turns out not to be about how many doors are open. It's about whether what you want is something you can actually have without betraying yourself. Third, the ladder. To make it vivid, he tells the story of a slave who longs to be freed. Once I'm free, he thinks, everything will be fine. He gets his freedom, and soon needs a patron to flatter for dinner. He climbs, saves, gets rich, maybe even rises to the senate. And at every rung he is serving someone, chasing someone's approval, more anxious than before. Epictetus says he's gone into a finer, fatter slavery. Fourth, the turn. Freedom, he concludes, is not won by getting everything you desire, but by removing the desire, the craving for what isn't yours to control. What's left is wanting what is in your own power, and holding the rest loosely. That isn't wanting nothing. It's wanting well. A person who wants to be honest today can be. A person who wants everyone to like them is at the mercy of everyone. Same person, same day. Different leash.
screen: `FREE: LIVING AS YOU WISH.` · `NO ONE WISHES TO LIVE IN ERROR.` · `THE FREED SLAVE'S LADDER.` · `NOT MORE DOORS: BETTER WANTS.` · then, large: `FREE IS WANTING RIGHTLY.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you want badly right now. A reply, a raise, someone's approval, a number on a scale. Hold it in mind. Now ask the Stoic question: which part of this is in my power? Maybe not the raise, but doing excellent work. Maybe not their reply, but how kindly you wrote. Let the want slide over onto that part, the part that's yours. Notice whether your shoulders change. Breathe with that smaller, steadier want. The bell holds the time.
Eleutheria. Greek for freedom: Epictetus' claim, On Freedom, that the free person lives as they wish, and the only way to do that is to wish for what is truly in their power.
Your line: same person, same day, different leash. Today, when a want starts pulling at you, move it one step, onto the piece that's yours to do. Day four hundred twenty-five.

426.title: Nothing to take
426.hook: no one could enslave Diogenes, because he'd let go of everything they could take
426.carry: how much of you someone could take
426.howItsDone: People who practice Stoicism sometimes rehearse letting go of possessions, roles or reputation in their minds, so that losing them would not mean losing themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday: eleutheria, Epictetus' long talk On Freedom, and your line, same person, same day, different leash. Did you move one want onto the part that was yours? Day four hundred twenty-six.

A pickpocket is working a crowded market. He's good. He reads people by what they clutch: the bag held tight, the hand that keeps checking the back pocket. Then he passes an old man in a torn cloak with an empty bag and a stick, sitting on the steps, laughing at something. The pickpocket walks right by. There is nothing to work with. Epictetus holds this old man, Diogenes, up as a picture of a free person, and he says why, in the middle of that same long talk on freedom. Today: Diogenes.
screen: `A PICKPOCKET READS WHAT YOU CLUTCH.` → `AN OLD MAN WITH AN EMPTY BAG.` → `NOTHING TO TAKE.`

segments.voice: First, the claim. In book four, chapter one, Epictetus says that from the day Diogenes learned from his teacher Antisthenes, no one could make him a slave again. Not because of his birth, not because of a document, but because of how he held things. Second, the handles. Here's a way to see it: everything you own has a handle. Your money has a handle. Your reputation has a handle. Even your body has one. Anyone who wants power over you just grabs the handle you care most about and pulls. In Epictetus' telling, Diogenes held his things so loosely that there was nothing for anyone to grab. Take the cloak, take the bag, even threaten the body: he'd give them up rather than give up himself. Third, the story people tell. Diogenes Laertius, a later collector of stories about the philosophers, says Diogenes was once captured by pirates and put up for sale. Asked what he could do, he said: govern men. Sell me, he said, to someone who needs a master. Nobody knows whether it happened. It's the kind of story that gets told about a person precisely because it fits. Fourth, the honest catch. This isn't a lesson in owning nothing. A life comes with kids, rent and a job, and Epictetus isn't asking anyone to walk away from them. The point is the grip. You can live in a house without being held by it. You can love a reputation without being leashed to it. The question is never how much you have. It's how much of you someone could take by taking it.

segments.voice: Make a fist with one hand, tight, as if you're holding something you're afraid to lose. Feel the strain in the fingers and the wrist. Name the thing, silently: my phone, my plans, what they think of me. Now slowly open the hand, palm up, and let it rest on your knee. The thing is still yours. You've only changed the grip. Breathe with your hand open. Notice that an open hand can still hold something, and can't be pried. The bell holds the time.
Diogenes. Epictetus' picture of a free person: he held everything so loosely that there was no handle left for anyone to grab.
Your line: how much of you someone could take. Pick one thing you grip too hard, a plan, a possession, a role, and loosen your hold on it once today. Day four hundred twenty-six.

427.title: My post
427.hook: stay at the post you've been given, like a soldier
427.howItsDone: Stoics often describe their daily responsibilities as a post they've been assigned, and try to carry them out fully and without complaint, wherever they happen to be.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Diogenes, with no handle left to grab, and your line, how much of you someone could take. Did you loosen your grip on one thing? Day four hundred twenty-seven. The end of a week.

It's three in the morning. A night nurse is the only person awake on the ward. Nothing is happening. Nobody will thank her for the next four hours, and if she wandered off for a while, maybe no one would notice. She stays. She walks the hall, checks the monitors, refills a water cup. Somewhere a lighthouse keeper once did the same, and a soldier at a gate, and a parent sitting up with a fever. Epictetus had a word for that kind of staying. It comes from the army, and it's in book three, chapter twenty-four, again. Today: my post.
screen: `THREE A.M. ON THE WARD.` → `NOBODY WATCHING. SHE STAYS.` → `MY POST.`

segments.voice: First, the picture. Epictetus says that each person's life is a kind of military service, and a long and varied one. In an army, he says, not everyone does the same job. One stands guard, one goes out to scout, one goes into battle. Not everyone can stay in one spot, and it wouldn't be better if they did. Each has a post. Second, the complaint. What ruins a soldier, he says, is grumbling at the general's orders: why me, why here, why the night shift. If everyone did that, nothing would get done, the camp wouldn't be guarded, the trench wouldn't be dug. The Stoics believed a reason runs through the whole of things, which they sometimes called God or Zeus, and that your post is part of it. Third, Socrates. The picture goes back to Plato's account of Socrates on trial, a speech Epictetus quotes elsewhere in the Discourses. Socrates told the jury that wherever a person has been stationed, they should stay and face the danger, as he had done as a soldier in three battles, and as he would now do at the post of philosophy, even if it cost his life. Fourth, the week. Look at what we gathered: alone, not lonely; a scout; in its season; at home here; free is wanting rightly; nothing to take. And now my post. Your post may be a cash register, a crib, a classroom, a hospital bed you're lying in. It's still a post.

segments.voice: Sit up a little, like someone on watch. Ask: what is my post today? Not your whole life. Just today. The meeting you have to run, the kid you're picking up, the shift, the long recovery. Name it plainly. Then notice any grumbling that comes with it, the why me. Don't argue with it. Just set it down beside you like a heavy bag. Breathe, and feel yourself standing where you've been put, steady, eyes open. The bell holds the time.
My post. Epictetus' soldier: each life has its own station, guard or scout or fighter, and the work is to stay at it well. Today's word.
Your line: stay at it well. Pick one job today you'd rather drift away from, and stay at it to the end, without grumbling. Day four hundred twenty-seven.
